verdict: Treat it as a candidate lesson. Every citation I could check resolves: the story's loop record (review/8) records the key-revocation stop, the concurrent run in which hidden-failure promoted and correctness was killed, and the detached re-run finishing in about eleven minutes; the correctness artifact's summary is timestamped 09:37 by the critic as claimed; this repo's BACKLOG.md matches the novelty claim (AAR-1 is the re-run-one-critic recovery that was used, OPS-3's 'key' hit is the hosted-runner note); the workflow repo's BACKLOG.md holds OPS-56, BUG-23 and OPS-71 as described and its .aar/rejected-lessons.md has no entries; /review step 8 does background the three critics in one shell with wait and says nothing about duration or caller ceilings; the stop vocabulary lists no class for the runner itself being terminated; and review_runner.py confirms the worktree cleanup lives in a finally with no signal handling, so an external kill bypasses it. The proposal is honest about what is session-observed (the orphan worktree, the first-attempt promotion times), names OPS-27's limit itself, engages a genuinely competing explanation, and declines to pick a remedy. The lesson is modest — much of the failure is the caller's ceiling, which the proposal concedes — but the two gaps it names (no stated budget, no cleanup or stop class for external termination) are real and verified.
contrary_evidence_omitted: None identified. I looked in the places most likely to cut against it: review_runner.py (it already runs `git worktree prune` only on the normal teardown path, never on start, so the proposal's third falsifier remains open; a comment near the stream-staging code already acknowledges 'Under SIGKILL no cleanup runs' for temp files, which supports rather than contradicts the cleanup half); both BACKLOG.md files and the rejected-lessons file (novelty claim holds); this round's own three artifacts (nothing in them conflicts with the account; the correctness artifact's 09:37 timestamp and 25-command count are consistent with a long detached run). The one thing no file can confirm — the exact 09:17 promotion time of the hidden-failure artifact on the concurrent run — is declared session-observed rather than asserted as durable, so it is not omitted evidence.
stronger_explanation: none — the proposal's explanation is the best available. Its competing 'caller's limitation' explanation is genuinely competing (a terminal caller has no cap and run_codex cannot prevent a SIGKILL) and the proposal correctly shows it does not cover the cleanup half: the runner's finally-based removal runs on no signal path, which I confirmed in the code, so even a catchable termination leaves the worktree. The lesson's narrow claim — no stated budget, no stop class, no cleanup-on-kill — is exactly what the evidence supports.

findings.title: 'The harness's maximum' collides with the loop's defined term
findings.claim: The proposal says the kill came from 'the caller's background time cap — ten minutes, the harness's maximum'. The workflow protocol defines 'reviewer harness' as codex/review_runner (workflow-protocol.md → Actors: 'A harness is not a reviewer; it enables them'), and review_runner has no ten-minute cap — the cap belongs to the desktop app's background shell that invoked the skill. A later reader of the workflow estate, where 'harness' already means something specific, could misread this as a limit inside run_codex.
findings.correction: Name the caller instead: 'the background shell's time cap — ten minutes, the desktop app's maximum for a backgrounded command'. The substance is unaffected; only the attribution needs one word changed.
